title: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users
author: Supreme Court of Victoria

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The Practice Note accepts the supervised-AI model and materially operationalises it for Victorian court proceedings. It preserves human responsibility, mandates meaningful verification of accuracy, completeness, currency and jurisdictional fit, distinguishes confidentiality controls for public and closed tools, and imposes heightened safeguards for witness and expert evidence. It does not assess whether verification costs consume efficiency gains, but concretely develops the cluster’s governance framework.

kp.k: AI assistance is permitted subject to court safeguards
kp.d: The Practice Note permits AI-assisted preparation of Court documents subject to compliance with its requirements and applies to all Court users from 14 May 2026, including lawyers, represented and self-represented litigants, and lay and expert witnesses. It states that AI can enhance access to justice and participation in Court processes; this is a stated potential benefit, not an empirical finding. Its guiding principles include fairness, accountability, privacy, transparency, procedural fairness, efficiency and human oversight.
qs: AI can enhance access to justice and Court users' participation in Court processes.
Court users can utilise AI in the preparation of Court documents if they comply with this Practice Note.
This Practice Note was issued and commences on 14 May 2026.
This Practice Note applies to all Court users.

kp.k: AI outputs create substantive legal and factual risks
kp.d: The Court warns that AI-generated material may be outdated, incomplete, inaccurate or inapplicable to the jurisdiction. It attributes risks to training-data biases, geographical information or misinformation, and statistical prediction without critical examination. It reports that reliance on fabricated cases, legislation or incorrect legal propositions has adversely affected Court users, without identifying incidents or supplying measured error rates.
qs: AI can produce outputs which are incorrect, biased and misleading.
It does not have an ability to critically examine the patterns it identifies in data.

the tool may not generate material addressing all arguments that a party is required to make or all issues that would be in a party's interests to cover, and summaries generated by such tools may not contain all relevant points.

the tool may not produce factually or legally correct output (for example, in some situations, Court users have been adversely affected by placing reliance on made-up cases, legislation or incorrect legal propositions).

kp.k: Responsibility remains with Court users despite AI assistance
kp.d: Court users remain responsible for their documents regardless of AI use and must avoid directly or indirectly misleading the Court or other litigation participants about AI-produced content or the nature of work undertaken. Civil proceedings remain subject to the Civil Procedure Act 2010 (Vic), including proper-basis certification. Inaccurate filings may result in costs orders.
qs: Court users are responsible for the content of their Court documents. This is the case whether or not a Court user has utilised AI.

Court users must be careful that their use of AI does not directly or indirectly mislead another participant in the litigation process or the Court about the nature of any work undertaken or the content produced by that AI tool.
Court users in civil proceedings are subject to the obligations imposed by the Civil Procedure Act 2010 (Vic), including certifying that claims have a proper basis.
Court users should be aware that filing a Court document which contains inaccuracies could result in costs orders.

kp.k: Lawyers retain independent judgment and face personal consequences
kp.d: AI-assisted legal tasks remain subject to lawyers' duties of competence, diligence, independent advice and candour. Lawyers must oversee AI use and verify both accuracy and suitability. Reliance on unverified outputs in Court documents may lead to referral to the Victorian Legal Services Board and Commissioner and personal costs orders; the Note states possible consequences rather than reporting enforcement outcomes.
qs: Lawyers should be aware that they have professional duties to act with competence and diligence, and to provide independent advice.
This means that irrespective of the AI tools used, lawyers must exercise oversight and verify the accuracy and suitability of the information provided by any AI system.
This includes the obligation of candour to the Court and, where applicable, to obligations imposed by the Civil Procedure Act 2010 (Vic).

Lawyers should be aware that if they rely on unverified AI outputs in Court documents they may be referred to the Victorian Legal Services Board and Commissioner and may be subject to personal costs orders.

kp.k: Confidentiality safeguards differ between public and closed AI
kp.d: The Note warns that some tools retain inputs for training or responses to other users. Court users should not enter confidential or sensitive information, including material covered by suppression or non-publication orders, into public AI tools, and lawyers must maintain client confidentiality. Closed AI is not treated as automatically secure: users entering protected information need to review contractual terms or privacy and confidentiality settings to satisfy themselves that inputs remain secure.
qs: Some AI tools retain the information you input and can use it to train the AI system and to respond to queries from other users.
Court users should not enter any information which is confidential or sensitive (including information subject to a non-publication or suppression order) into a public AI tool.
Lawyers must comply with their obligations to maintain client confidentiality.

If Court users input private, confidential or sensitive information into closed AI tools they need to exercise caution and satisfy themselves by reviewing the contractual terms or privacy and confidentiality settings that the information they input will be kept within a secure environment.

kp.k: AI-assisted evidence must preserve witnesses' knowledge and words
kp.d: The Court requires particular caution when GenAI assists with affidavits, witness statements or other potential witness evidence. Finalised or sworn material must reflect the person's own knowledge and words. AI assistance with expert reports also calls for particular caution, and reports must comply with the applicable Code of Conduct or Practice Note.
qs: Particular caution must be exercised if GenAI tools are used to assist in the preparation of affidavit materials, witness statements or other documents which form the evidence or potential evidence of a witness.
The relevant Court user must ensure that Court documents are sworn/affirmed or finalised in a form that reflects that person's own knowledge and words.
Particular caution must be exercised if AI is used to assist in the preparation of an expert report. Expert reports must be prepared in compliance with the relevant Code of Conduct or Practice Note.

kp.k: Meaningful human verification is required before reliance
kp.d: AI-produced content must undergo verification with meaningful human control. Court users must ensure currency, completeness, accuracy and jurisdictional applicability and should review for bias and discrimination. For GenAI material submitted to the Court, the Note recommends fact-checking, proofreading, adaptation and checking both the existence of authorities and whether they support the attributed propositions. Quotations and extracts must also be checked for accuracy and attribution.
qs: Content produced using AI must be verified with meaningful human control.
Court users are responsible for ensuring that content produced by AI is current, complete, accurate and applicable to the jurisdiction.
Court users should be alert to the risk of bias and discrimination when reviewing AI outputs.

Verify that any references to case law, legislation, textbooks or articles exist and stand for the legal positions attributed to them. Any extracts or quotes must be verified as accurate and attributed to the correct source.

kp.k: AI confirmation cannot replace checking reliable original sources
kp.d: The Note distinguishes genuine source verification from asking AI to confirm its own or another tool's generated material. It permits checking original source material housed within a GenAI tool, but not using one AI tool to confirm another's generated content. It directs users toward sources known to be accurate and specifically identifies AustLII, authorised legislation websites and Law Library Victoria resources for self-represented litigants.
qs: For self-represented litigants, this includes AustLII for case law, authorised websites for legislation, and resources available from the Law Library Victoria.
Note that it is not sufficient verification to ask an AI tool to confirm that the materials exist or contain the content that GenAI says they do.
One AI tool cannot be used to confirm the content generated by another AI tool.
However, Court users may verify GenAI content by referring to original source material housed within a GenAI tool.

kp.k: Court users must explain AI contributions and verification
kp.d: The Court may request further information about AI-assisted documents. Users must be prepared to identify the specific portions produced using AI and explain their verification process. These provisions establish preparedness for Court scrutiny, rather than expressly requiring routine disclosure of every AI use.
qs: The Court may direct Court users to provide further information about Court documents they have produced with the assistance of AI.
Court users must be prepared to identify the specific portions of Court documents which were produced using AI and be able to explain how the output was verified.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Supreme Court of Victoria presents AI as potentially improving access to justice and participation, while permitting its use in document preparation subject to safeguards.
pts.d: The Court's Practice Note makes a qualified claim about AI's benefits rather than predicting quantified gains. It identifies risks of outdated, incomplete, inaccurate, biased or jurisdictionally inappropriate content, including fabricated legal authorities, and risks to confidentiality. Its prescribed approach is human-supervised assistance: AI does not transfer responsibility away from Court users, and lawyers must verify accuracy and suitability. AI-assisted evidence must preserve the witness's own knowledge and words. Reliance on unverified outputs can expose lawyers to regulatory referral and personal costs orders. These are statements of potential benefits, risks and procedural requirements, not forecasts of employment or legal-market change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source supplies judicial and legal authority, qualitative explanations of AI risks, and an unspecified reference to adverse incidents; it offers no quantitative evaluation.
pts.d: The Practice Note is authorised by the Chief Justice. Its guiding principles draw on the Victorian Law Reform Commission's October 2025 report. It anchors users' responsibilities in the Civil Procedure Act 2010 (Vic), lawyers' professional duties and applicable expert-evidence rules. For technical risks it offers explanations involving training data, statistical prediction and information retention. It mentions adverse effects from fabricated cases, legislation or incorrect propositions without identifying particular proceedings. No data, benchmarks or measured effect sizes are supplied for either access-to-justice benefits or error risks. The cited legal obligations establish the normative basis of the requirements rather than empirical proof of AI's effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The requirements commence on 14 May 2026; benefits and risks are framed as present possibilities, with use conditional on meaningful human verification.
pts.d: The Note replaces the May 2024 guidelines and does not give a future horizon for technological or market developments. Court users must check currency, completeness, accuracy and jurisdictional applicability. Verification must include checking authorities and quotations against reliable sources: asking an AI tool to confirm generated content is insufficient, although consulting original source material housed within a GenAI tool is permitted. Public tools should not receive confidential or sensitive information; use of closed tools requires checking contractual terms or privacy and confidentiality settings. Users must be able to identify AI-produced portions and explain their verification if required.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The Note covers all Court users, with additional professional obligations for lawyers and specific safeguards for witnesses, experts and confidential client information.
pts.d: Lawyers, represented and self-represented litigants, and lay and expert witnesses fall within its scope. All users retain responsibility for documents and risk costs orders for inaccuracies. Lawyers additionally face professional oversight, confidentiality duties and potential personal costs consequences. Witnesses must retain ownership of the substance and wording of evidence, while experts must comply with applicable codes and practice notes. Self-represented litigants are directed to accessible authoritative resources for verification. Other litigation participants and the Court are protected by the requirement not to mislead them about AI-assisted work. The source does not distinguish law-firm sizes, ALSPs or other legal-market segments.
